short.title: Our Schools Were Built on Three Old Models
short.text:
The factory. The prison. The church.

In The Future Ready Challenge I wrote that our schools were shaped by all three: uniformity, compliance, and discipline. A lot of that design is still running in our buildings today.

Our kids don't need more practice standing in line. They need practice standing out.

linkedin.text:
In The Future Ready Challenge, I argued that our school system was shaped by three models: the factory, the prison, and the church.

From the factory we took uniformity: bells, batches, and age-based grades.
From the prison we took compliance: lines, hall passes, and quiet hallways.
From the church we took discipline: sit still, listen, and don't question.

Some of that served a purpose in its time. But we're now preparing children for work that hasn't been invented yet, and compliance alone won't get them there.

The change doesn't have to start with a new building or a new board policy. It can start with one lesson. Take something you already teach and redesign it so students create, investigate, or argue a position instead of copying notes.

If time is the barrier (and it usually is), VIC, the free tool I built for teachers, can draft that redesign from a lesson you already have.

short.title: Feedback That Helps People Grow
short.text:
"Criticism, like rain, should be gentle enough to nourish growth without destroying roots." 🌧️🌱

Compliment. Suggestion. Correction. It's how I teach peer review to kids, and how I try to give feedback to adults.

Swipe for the 3 steps. Which one do you skip most? 👇

#teachersofinstagram #teachertok #feedback #schoolleadership #principallife #classroomculture

linkedin.text:
"Criticism, like rain, should be gentle enough to nourish growth without destroying roots."

I quoted that line in The Future Ready Challenge because I think we've lost the art of constructive feedback. Online, we tear each other down. In schools, we often swing the other way and say nothing useful at all.

The structure I teach students for peer review works just as well in a post-observation conversation:

1. Compliment: name something specific that works.
2. Suggestion: offer one "what if" that could make it stronger.
3. Correction: if something is wrong, say it plainly and kindly.

Kids who learn this become adults who can disagree without going for the jugular. Leaders who model it build staff who actually want feedback.

short.title: The Best Lesson Isn't Always in the Book
short.text:
Just because a lesson is in the book doesn't mean it's the best lesson for YOUR students. 📚

The lessons kids remember come from a teacher who knows them, not from a table of contents.

Teachers: what's one lesson you wrote yourself that your students still talk about? 👇

#teachersofinstagram #teachertok #teacherlife #lessonplanning #education

linkedin.text:
"Just because a lesson is found in a book doesn't mean it's the best lesson for your students."

I wrote that in The Future Ready Challenge, and it still gets a reaction from teachers, both nods and pushback.

To be clear, curriculum matters. Pacing guides and adopted materials exist for good reasons. But the textbook was written for an imaginary average class. The teacher is the only one who knows the actual kids in the room.

The best lessons usually start with the standard and the curriculum, then take a turn only that teacher could take: a local connection, a student's obsession, a real problem to solve.

Leaders: how much room does your building give teachers to take that turn?

#Teaching #Curriculum #SchoolLeadership #FutureReady

days.label: What would you do? The Sick Note

short.title: Principals: Excused or Unexcused?
short.text:
Principals and teachers: what would you do? 🤔

A mom sends a sick note. Her daughter isn't sick. She was so scared of a doctor visit and a shot that Mom let her stay home. Later, Mom calls and tells you the truth, and asks you not to count it against her daughter.

Excused or unexcused? Comment your call. What I did is in the first comment.

Practice decisions like this in my free principal simulation: drrobfurman.com (link in bio)

#principal #principallife #teachertok #teachersofinstagram #schoolleadership
short.first_comment: What I did: I thanked her for telling the truth and kept the absence excused. A child that scared of a doctor visit and a shot was, in a real sense, sick. This was a good family, not one trying to beat the system, and I wanted her honesty to lead to a better outcome. I also made clear she should tell us the real story next time. Attendance rules matter. So does knowing when honesty deserves grace.

linkedin.text:
A leadership scenario from my "What Would You Do?" collection. Details changed for privacy.

A parent sends a note saying her daughter is sick. She isn't. The girl was so anxious about a possible doctor visit and a shot that her mother let her stay home. They never went to the doctor.

Later, the mother calls back. She feels guilty. She tells you exactly what happened and worries the unexcused mark will count against her daughter.

The by-the-book answer: unexcused. The note was false.
The human answer: excused. The anxiety was real, and the mother came clean.

I'll share what I chose in the comments. First, what would you do, and why?

If you want to practice calls like this, my free simulation "A Day in the Life of a Principal" puts you in the chair for a full day: https://www.drrobfurman.com/human-equation-suite/leadership-sim

#SchoolLeadership #Principals #AspiringPrincipals #EducationalLeadership
linkedin.first_comment: What I chose: I thanked the mother for telling the truth and kept the absence excused. A child who had worked herself into that level of anxiety was, in a real sense, sick. This was a good family, not one trying to beat the system, and I wanted honesty to lead to a better outcome, while making clear she should tell us the real story next time. Use judgment, reward honesty, keep the door open.

short.title: Kids Know Movie Release Dates. What About Books?
short.text:
Your kid can tell you when the next big movie comes out. Can they name one new book? 🎬📚

That's not a character flaw. Movies and games are marketed to kids everywhere. Books mostly aren't. You can't be interested in something you don't know exists.

short.title: The Word Follower Becomes Obsolete
short.text:
In the 21st century, the word "follower" becomes obsolete.

On real teams, everyone has to step up and lead at some point. Let's raise kids who are ready for that moment, not kids who only know how to wait for directions.

From my book The Future Ready Challenge. Follow for more from the principal's chair. 🎙️
